claim: Axolotls are able to resolve spinal cord injuries.
source: Axolotls are uniquely able to resolve spinal cord injuries, but little is known about the mechanisms underlying spinal cord regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about axolotls.

claim: Tail amputation leads to reactivation of a developmental-like program in spinal cord ependymal cells.
source: We previously found that tail amputation leads to reactivation of a developmental-like program in spinal cord ependymal cells (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015), characterized by a high-proliferation zone emerging 4 days post-amputation (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: A high-proliferation zone emerges 4 days post-amputation in the spinal cord.
source: We previously found that tail amputation leads to reactivation of a developmental-like program in spinal cord ependymal cells (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015), characterized by a high-proliferation zone emerging 4 days post-amputation (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The regenerative response is consistent with a signal that recruits ependymal cells during ~85 hours after amputation within ~830 μm of the injury.
source: Here, we use modeling, tightly linked to experimental data, to demonstrate that this regenerative response is consistent with a signal that recruits ependymal cells during ~85 hours after amputation within ~830 μm of the injury.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on modeling and experimental data.

claim: AxFUCCI axolotls confirmed the predicted appearance time and size of the injury-induced recruitment zone.
source: AxFUCCI axolotls confirmed the predicted appearance time and size of the injury-induced recruitment zone and revealed cell cycle synchrony between ependymal cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental validation using the AxFUCCI system.

claim: AxFUCCI axolotls revealed cell cycle synchrony between ependymal cells.
source: AxFUCCI axolotls confirmed the predicted appearance time and size of the injury-induced recruitment zone and revealed cell cycle synchrony between ependymal cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental observations using AxFUCCI.

claim: Ependymal cells lining the central canal of the spinal cord retain neural stem cell potential throughout life.
source: Key players in this process are the ependymal cells lining the central canal of the spinal cord, which retain neural stem cell potential throughout life (Becker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Spinal cord injury in the axolotl triggers the reactivation of a developmental-like program in ependymal cells, including a switch from slow, neurogenic to fast, proliferative cell divisions.
source: In earlier studies, we found that spinal cord injury in the axolotl triggers the reactivation of a developmental-like program in ependymal cells, including a switch from slow, neurogenic to fast, proliferative cell divisions (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In the uninjured spinal cord, ependymal cells divide slowly, completing a cell cycle in 14.2 ± 1.3 days.
source: We showed that in the uninjured spinal cord and in the non-regenerating region of the injured spinal cord, ependymal cells divide slowly, completing a cell cycle in 14.2 ± 1.3 days.
evidence: This claim is based on previous experimental measurements by the authors.

claim: Regenerating ependymal cells divide every 4.9 ± 0.4 days.
source: In contrast, regenerating ependymal cells speed up their cell cycle and divide every 4.9 ± 0.4 days (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015; Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on previous experimental measurements by the authors.

claim: The acceleration of the cell cycle is the major driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth.
source: By using a mathematical modeling approach, we demonstrated that the acceleration of the cell cycle is the major driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth and that other processes such as cell influx, cell rearrangements, and neural stem cell activation from quiescence play smaller roles (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on previous modeling work by the authors.

claim: A high-proliferation zone emerges 4 days after amputation within the 800 μm adjacent to the injury site.
source: We quantitatively analyzed cell proliferation in space and time and identified a high-proliferation zone that emerges 4 days after amputation within the 800 μm adjacent to the injury site and shifts posteriorly over time as the regenerating spinal cord grows (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on previous quantitative analysis by the authors.

claim: The high-proliferation zone shifts posteriorly over time as the regenerating spinal cord grows.
source: We quantitatively analyzed cell proliferation in space and time and identified a high-proliferation zone that emerges 4 days after amputation within the 800 μm adjacent to the injury site and shifts posteriorly over time as the regenerating spinal cord grows (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on previous quantitative analysis by the authors.

claim: The model successfully reproduced the experimental switchpoint with best-fitting parameters N0 = 196 ± 2 cells, λ = 828 ± 30 μm, and τ = 85 ± 12 hours.
source: The model successfully reproduced the experimental switchpoint with best-fitting parameters N0 = 196 ± 2 cells, λ = 828 ± 30 μm, and τ = 85 ± 12 hours (Figure 2A; parameter posterior distributions obtained after convergence are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and see Section 1.3 for details).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on model fitting to experimental data, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Cells located close to the amputation plane end up at the posterior end of the regenerated spinal cord.
source: Interestingly, a clonal analysis of the model shows that while the anterior-most cells are slightly displaced, cells located close to the amputation plane end up at the posterior end of the regenerated spinal cord (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), in agreement with cell trajectories observed during axolotl spinal cord regeneration (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations that agrees with previous experimental observations.

claim: The velocity of a clone monotonically increases with its AP coordinate.
source: Additionally, the velocity of a clone monotonically increases with its AP coordinate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), also in line with experimental data (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations that agrees with previous experimental data.

claim: Cells preserve their relative position along the AP axis during regeneration.
source: These results suggest that cells preserve their relative position along the AP axis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results.

claim: The model quantitatively predicted the time evolution of the regenerative outgrowth that was observed in vivo.
source: Importantly, with the parameterization leading to the best fitting of the experimental switchpoint, we quantitatively predicted the time evolution of the regenerative outgrowth that was observed in vivo (Rost et al., 2016; Figure 2B, Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding showing agreement between model predictions and experimental observations.

claim: Blocking recruitment and the acceleration of the cell cycle slows down tissue growth, leading to an outgrowth of 694 ± 77 μm instead of the observed 1127 ± 103 μm at day 6.
source: Our results show that blocking recruitment, and therefore the acceleration of the cell cycle, slows down tissue growth, leading to an outgrowth of 694 ± 77 μm instead of the observed 1127 ± 103 μm at day 6 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model when cell cycle acceleration is blocked.

claim: The model-predicted outgrowth when cell cycle acceleration is blocked is in agreement with the reported experimental outgrowth in Sox2 knock-out axolotls.
source: Interestingly, this model-predicted outgrowth is in agreement with the reported experimental outgrowth in Sox2 knock-out axolotls, in which the acceleration of the cell cycle does not take place after amputation (Figure 2C, Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental data from a different study.

claim: Shortening of only S phase can explain the explosive spinal cord outgrowth observed in vivo, independently of G1 shortening, up to day 4.
source: Interestingly, our results indicate that shortening of only S phase can explain the explosive spinal cord outgrowth observed in vivo, independently of G1 shortening, up to day 4 (Figure 2D, blue line and orange line).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations testing different scenarios.

claim: Shortening of only G1 phase has a mild impact on the initial outgrowth.
source: In contrast, shortening of only G1 phase has a mild impact on the initial outgrowth as it results in an outgrowth almost identical to the case in which neither G1 nor S phase was reduced (Figure 2D, magenta line versus green line).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations testing different scenarios.

claim: From day 4, shortening of both S and G1 phases is necessary to recapitulate the observed outgrowth.
source: From day 4, though, shortening of only S phase cannot recapitulate the observed outgrowth (Figure 2D, blue line and orange line), and indeed, it is the shortening of both S and G1 phases that returns the same outgrowth than that observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations testing different scenarios.

claim: Up to day 4, shortening of S phase can explain the regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in the axolotl, while the effect of G1 shortening manifests from day 5.
source: To conclude, these results indicate that, up to day 4, shortening of S phase can explain the regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in the axolotl, while the effect of G1 shortening manifests from day 5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: AxFUCCI fluorescence oscillated during the cell cycle in the order mVenus > Double positive > mCherry > Double positive > mVenus.
source: As expected, AxFUCCI fluorescence oscillated during the cell cycle in the order mVenus > Double positive > mCherry > Double positive > mVenus (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B, Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from live-cell imaging.

claim: mVenus-positive cells were G0/G1 cells and mCherry-positive cells were S/G2 cells.
source: We confirmed that mVenus-positive cells were G0/G1 cells and that mCherry-positive cells were S/G2 cells using a flow cytometer to analyze DNA content (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental validation using flow cytometry.

claim: Cells are transiently AxFUCCI double positive between G0/G1 and S/G2, corresponding to the G1/S boundary.
source: Cells are transiently AxFUCCI double positive between G0/G1 and S/G2 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B); we infer that these cells are at the G1/S boundary, as observed in mouse FUCCI (Abe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and comparison to mouse FUCCI.

claim: A second AxFUCCI double-positive window exists between S/G2 and G0/G1, corresponding to the G2/M boundary and M cells.
source: Interestingly, and in contrast to FUCCI in other model organisms, we observe a second AxFUCCI double-positive window between S/G2 and G0/G1, corresponding to the G2/M boundary and M cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation that differs from FUCCI in other organisms.

claim: AxFUCCI discriminates the following cell cycle phases in axolotl: G0/G1 (mVenus only); S/G2 (mCherry only); G1/S transition and G2/M transition (double positive).
source: Thus, AxFUCCI discriminates the following cell cycle phases in axolotl: G0/G1 (mVenus only); S/G2 (mCherry only); G1/S transition and G2/M transition (double positive) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental validation of AxFUCCI.

claim: AxFUCCI animals developed at a similar rate to their non-transgenic siblings.
source: AxFUCCI animals developed at a similar rate to their non-transgenic siblings, did not differ in their basal cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), and regenerated amputated tail tissue with similar kinetics to the d/d animals used in our previous study (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation validating that AxFUCCI does not affect normal development.

claim: AxFUCCI animals did not differ in their basal cell proliferation compared to controls.
source: AxFUCCI animals developed at a similar rate to their non-transgenic siblings, did not differ in their basal cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), and regenerated amputated tail tissue with similar kinetics to the d/d animals used in our previous study (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation validating that AxFUCCI does not affect basal proliferation.

claim: AxFUCCI animals regenerated amputated tail tissue with similar kinetics to the d/d animals used in the previous study.
source: AxFUCCI animals developed at a similar rate to their non-transgenic siblings, did not differ in their basal cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), and regenerated amputated tail tissue with similar kinetics to the d/d animals used in our previous study (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation validating that AxFUCCI does not affect regeneration kinetics.

claim: mCherry-positive cells harbored significantly more DNA than mVenus-positive cells.
source: As expected, mCherry-positive cells harbored significantly more DNA than mVenus-positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental validation using DNA content analysis.

claim: Following an 8 hours EdU pulse, mCherry-positive cells but not mVenus-positive cells were EdU-positive.
source: Thirdly, we injected AxFUCCI axolotls intraperitoneally with EdU, a thymidine analogue that is incorporated into DNA during S phase. Following an 8 hours EdU pulse, mCherry-positive cells but not mVenus-positive cells should be EdU-positive and this was indeed the case (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is an experimental validation using EdU incorporation.

claim: 100% of neurons that expressed AxFUCCI were mVenus-positive.
source: NeuN-expressing neurons, located on the periphery of the spinal cord, are post-mitotic, differentiated cells (G0) and should be mVenus-positive (and never mCherry-positive). Indeed, we found that 100% of neurons that expressed AxFUCCI were mVenus-positive (Figure 3—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: This is an experimental validation using cell type-specific markers.

claim: Sox2-expressing ependymal cells expressed mVenus, mCherry, or both fluorophores.
source: By contrast, Sox2-expressing ependymal cells, which are proliferative cells, expressed mVenus, mCherry, or both fluorophores (Figure 3—figure supplement 4H).
evidence: This is an experimental validation using cell type-specific markers.

claim: At amputation, most ependymal cells expressed G0/G1-AxFUCCI and only a minority expressed S/G2-AxFUCCI.
source: We found that, at amputation, most ependymal cells expressed G0/G1-AxFUCCI and only a minority expressed S/G2-AxFUCCI (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from AxFUCCI animals.

claim: In the 5 days following tail tip amputation, the proportion of S/G2-AxFUCCI-expressing cells increased locally and sharply at the amputation site, then propagated anteriorly along the spinal cord.
source: In the 5 days following tail tip amputation, the proportion of S/G2-AxFUCCI-expressing cells increased locally and sharply at the amputation site, then propagated anteriorly along the spinal cord, consistent with the appearance of a recruitment zone (Figures 1B and 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from AxFUCCI animals.

claim: The AP border of the AxFUCCI data was measured to be at –717 ± 272 μm relative to the amputation plane on day 4 and –446 ± 112 μm on day 5.
source: Crucially, we measured the AP border of the AxFUCCI data to be at –717 ± 272 μm relative to the amputation plane on day 4 and –446 ± 112 μm on day 5, overlapping within 2 sigma the –782 ± 50 μm and –710 ± 62 μm recruitment limits predicted by our model (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from AxFUCCI data that validates model predictions.

claim: The AP border of the AxFUCCI data overlaps within 2 sigma the recruitment limits predicted by the model.
source: Crucially, we measured the AP border of the AxFUCCI data to be at –717 ± 272 μm relative to the amputation plane on day 4 and –446 ± 112 μm on day 5, overlapping within 2 sigma the –782 ± 50 μm and –710 ± 62 μm recruitment limits predicted by our model (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a comparison showing agreement between experimental data and model predictions.

claim: The appearance of the recruitment zone between days 3 and 4 post-amputation accommodates the 85 hours recruitment time in the model.
source: Moreover, the appearance of the recruitment zone between days 3 and 4 post-amputation accommodates the 85 hours recruitment time in our model.
evidence: This is a comparison showing agreement between experimental observations and model predictions.

claim: AxFUCCI animals confirmed the predicted appearance time and size of the recruitment zone.
source: Thus, AxFUCCI animals confirmed the predicted appearance time and size of the recruitment zone.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the validation of model predictions.

claim: At the moment of amputation, 85% ± 5% of ependymal cells expressed G0/G1-AxFUCCI and 11% ± 6% expressed S/G2-AxFUCCI.
source: At the moment of amputation, 85% ± 5% of ependymal cells expressed G0/G1-AxFUCCI and 11% ± 6% expressed S/G2-AxFUCCI (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from AxFUCCI animals.

claim: A significant drop in G0/G1-AxFUCCI-expressing ependymal cells was detected at day 1 post-amputation.
source: After amputation, we detected a significant drop in G0/G1-AxFUCCI-expressing ependymal cells already at day 1.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of AxFUCCI data.

claim: The number of S/G2-AxFUCCI-expressing cells increased significantly starting at 3 days and reached 50% at days 4 and 5 post-amputation.
source: Reciprocally, the number of S/G2-AxFUCCI-expressing cells increased significantly starting at 3 days and reached 50% at days 4 and 5 post-amputation, compared to a baseline percentage below 10% (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of AxFUCCI data.

claim: M phase cells started to appear noticeably from day 4 post-amputation.
source: M phase cells started to appear noticeably from day 4, although it was not possible to perform statistical analysis due to the absence of M phase cells in the 0 day post-amputation samples (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from AxFUCCI data.

claim: A transient 'burst' of Transition-AxFUCCI cells occurred at days 1 and 2 post-amputation.
source: Intriguingly, we observed a transient 'burst' of Transition-AxFUCCI cells at days 1 and 2 post-amputation. The percentage of Transition-AxFUCCI cells increased to 21% ± 12% and 23% ± 12%, respectively, during this burst, before declining back to the baseline level of 5% ± 4% at 3 days (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of AxFUCCI data.

claim: Transition-AxFUCCI cells at 1 and 2 days post-amputation were almost entirely EdU-negative and therefore resided in G1/S.
source: Consistent with our expectations, Transition-AxFUCCI cells at 1 and 2 days post-amputation were almost entirely EdU-negative and therefore resided in G1/S (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from EdU incorporation experiments.

claim: Following tail amputation, ependymal cells start to leave G0/G1 within the first day of amputation, transit through G1/S at days 1 and 2, enter S/G2 from day 3 onwards, and undergo mitosis from day 4.
source: In sum, AxFUCCI revealed the following cell cycle dynamics during regeneration (summarized in Figure 5E). Most ependymal cells in the uninjured spinal cord reside in G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle. Following tail amputation, ependymal cells start to leave G0/G1 within the first day of amputation, transit through G1/S at days 1 and 2, enter S/G2 from day 3 onwards, and undergo mitosis from day 4.
evidence: This is a summary of the cell cycle dynamics observed using AxFUCCI.

claim: The 4.5-fold increase in Transition-AxFUCCI-expressing cells at days 1 and 2 post-amputation is a strong indication of cell cycle synchrony during early spinal cord regeneration.
source: We take the 4.5-fold increase in Transition-AxFUCCI-expressing cells at days 1 and 2 post-amputation as a strong indication of cell cycle synchrony during early spinal cord regeneration, a key prediction of our model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the AxFUCCI data as evidence for cell cycle synchrony.

claim: The speed of spinal cord tissue regeneration was similar between AxFUCCI animals and the animals from the previous study despite differences in baseline cell cycle conditions.
source: Despite these differences, we found the speed of spinal cord tissue regeneration to be similar in the two datasets (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B). This could reflect a convergence in regenerative response at the cell cycle level.
evidence: This is an observation comparing regeneration kinetics between different datasets.

claim: Simulated G1-to-S transitions were more frequent posterior to the experimentally derived recruitment limit.
source: We validated the simulations by testing where and when ependymal cells would leave G1 phase to enter S phase and found that, as expected, simulated G1-to-S transitions were more frequent posterior to the experimentally derived recruitment limit (Figure 6E), which at days 4 and 5 overlap with the determined AP borders.
evidence: This is a validation of model simulations against experimental data.

claim: Simulated cell divisions exhibited a similar pattern to G1-to-S transitions, being more frequent posterior to the recruitment limit.
source: Consequently, simulated cell divisions (M phase) exhibited a similar pattern (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations.

claim: The cell cycle conditions at day 0 differ between the AxFUCCI experiments and the model but match quantitatively at day 4 post-amputation.
source: As noted, the cell cycle conditions at day 0 differ between the AxFUCCI experiments and our model but match quantitatively at day 4 post-amputation (Figure 6A–D, Video 5).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and model simulations.

claim: The appearance of the recruitment zone was later in the AxFUCCI animals (days 4–5) than in the simulations (day 2).
source: We found the appearance of the recruitment zone to be later in the AxFUCCI animals (days 4–5) than in the simulations (day 2).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental observations and model simulations.

claim: Once the recruitment zone is evident in the AxFUCCI data, its size at days 4 and 5 is comparable to the one predicted by the simulations at those times.
source: However, once the recruitment zone is evident in the AxFUCCI data, its size at days 4 and 5 is comparable to the one predicted by the simulations at those times.
evidence: This is a comparison showing agreement between experimental data and model predictions.

claim: The recruitment zone in the AxFUCCI spinal cord manifests more synchronously and rapidly than in the simulations.
source: Thus, the recruitment zone in the AxFUCCI spinal cord manifests more synchronously and rapidly than in the simulations, in which it increases gradually in size in a posterior-to-anterior direction between days 2 and 4.
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental observations and model simulations.

claim: The larger pool of G0/G1 cells in the AxFUCCI animals at days 0–2 compared to the model incurs a collective but relatively synchronous lag in S phase entry.
source: This is likely a consequence of the larger pool of G0/G1 cells in the AxFUCCI animals at days 0–2 compared to the model, which incurs a collective (but relatively synchronous) lag in S phase entry (recruitment zone manifestation).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences between experimental data and model simulations.

claim: The spatiotemporal pattern of cell proliferation in the regenerating axolotl spinal cord is consistent with a signal that propagates anteriorly 828 µm from the injury site during the first 85 hours post-amputation.
source: Here, by using a modeling approach tightly linked to experimental data, we find that the spatiotemporal pattern of cell proliferation in the regenerating axolotl spinal cord is consistent with a signal that propagates anteriorly 828 µm from the injury site during the first 85 hours post-amputation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on modeling and experimental validation.

claim: Shortening of S phase is sufficient to explain the explosive growth observed during the first days of regeneration.
source: We show that shortening of S phase is sufficient to explain the explosive growth observed during the first days of regeneration, but that both S and G1 shortening are necessary to explain/sustain further outgrowth before the first newborn neurons are seen (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations.

claim: Both S and G1 shortening are necessary to explain/sustain further outgrowth before the first newborn neurons are seen.
source: We show that shortening of S phase is sufficient to explain the explosive growth observed during the first days of regeneration, but that both S and G1 shortening are necessary to explain/sustain further outgrowth before the first newborn neurons are seen (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations.

claim: Regulation of G1 and S phases are well-known mechanisms controlling cell fate and cell output in a number of developmental contexts.
source: Regulation of G1 and S phases are well-known mechanisms controlling cell fate and cell output in a number of developmental contexts.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the brain, G1 lengthening results in longer cell cycles in neural progenitors undergoing neurogenesis.
source: In the brain, G1 lengthening results in longer cell cycles in neural progenitors undergoing neurogenesis (Lukaszewicz et al., 2005; Calegari et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 1995), while experimental shortening of G1 in neural progenitors of the cerebral cortex results in more proliferative divisions, increasing the progenitor pool and delaying neurogenesis (Salomoni and Calegari, 2010; Lange et al., 2009; Pilaz et al., 2009; Calegari and Huttner, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Experimental shortening of G1 in neural progenitors of the cerebral cortex results in more proliferative divisions, increasing the progenitor pool and delaying neurogenesis.
source: In the brain, G1 lengthening results in longer cell cycles in neural progenitors undergoing neurogenesis (Lukaszewicz et al., 2005; Calegari et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 1995), while experimental shortening of G1 in neural progenitors of the cerebral cortex results in more proliferative divisions, increasing the progenitor pool and delaying neurogenesis (Salomoni and Calegari, 2010; Lange et al., 2009; Pilaz et al., 2009; Calegari and Huttner, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The shortening of G1 during spinal cord regeneration is necessary to sustain the expansion of the ependymal cell pool.
source: Here, we have shown that the shortening of G1 during spinal cord regeneration is necessary to sustain the expansion of the ependymal cell pool.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The regulation of G1 length is a key mechanism regulating the output of neural stem/progenitor cell divisions in development and in regeneration.
source: Together, these findings point to the regulation of G1 length as a key mechanism regulating the output of neural stem/progenitor cell divisions in development and in regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and comparison to previous work.

claim: The length of S phase is regulated during development by modulating the number of DNA replication origins.
source: The length of S phase is also regulated during development by modulating the number of DNA replication origins (Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In mammals, mouse neural progenitors committed to neurogenesis and neurogenic cortical progenitors in the ferret undergo shorter S phase than their self-renewing/proliferative counterparts.
source: In mammals, shortening of S phase seems to play a role in regulating the mode of cell division: mouse neural progenitors committed to neurogenesis and neurogenic cortical progenitors in the ferret undergo shorter S phase than their self-renewing/proliferative counterparts (Turrero García et al., 2016; Arai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the axolotl, regenerating ependymal cells shorten S phase during the expansion/outgrowth phase.
source: In the axolotl, regenerating ependymal cells shorten S phase during the expansion/outgrowth phase.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The regulation of S phase controls cell output in the context of development and regeneration rather than influence the mode of cell division.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the regulation of S phase controls cell output in the context of development and regeneration rather than influence the mode of cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing findings across different contexts.

claim: The combined shortening of S and G1 in the regenerating spinal cord sustains the expansion of the resident ependymal/neural stem cell pool at the expense of neurogenesis.
source: The combined shortening of S and G1 in the regenerating spinal cord sustains the expansion of the resident ependymal/neural stem cell pool at the expense of neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Experimentally shortening G1 and S phases in cortical progenitors of the developing mouse brain delayed the onset of neurogenesis.
source: In this line, experimentally shortening G1 and S phases in cortical progenitors of the developing mouse brain delayed the onset of neurogenesis (Hasenpusch-Theil et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cell cycle regulation is a key mechanism controlling the number and type of cells needed to generate and regenerate a tissue.
source: Our findings add to the evidence that cell cycle regulation is a key mechanism controlling the number and type of cells needed to generate and regenerate a tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and comparison to previous work.

claim: A signal must spread about 800 μm from the injury site while recruiting ependymal cells during the 85 hours after amputation to explain the spatiotemporal pattern of cell proliferation in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Another prediction of our model is that a signal must spread about 800 μm from the injury site while recruiting ependymal cells during the 85 hours after amputation to explain the spatiotemporal pattern of cell proliferation in the regenerating spinal cord.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: There was remarkable agreement between the model prediction and the size and timing of appearance of the recruitment zone in AxFUCCI spinal cords.
source: In order to test this prediction experimentally, we adapted FUCCI technology to axolotls, which enabled us to visualize cell cycle dynamics in vivo. We found remarkable agreement between our prediction and the size and timing of appearance of the recruitment zone in AxFUCCI spinal cords.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation of model predictions using AxFUCCI.

claim: The size of the recruitment zone appears similar between 3 cm and 5.5 cm axolotls.
source: Our prediction was made based on data from 3 cm snout-to-tail axolotls, while the AxFUCCI measurements were taken from 5.5 cm axolotls. That the size of the recruitment zone appears similar between these two animal sizes could be important in understanding the identity of the injury-induced signal and how it spreads to recruit ependymal cells.
evidence: This is an observation comparing results from different animal sizes.

claim: Cell cycle synchronization is difficult to measure in cells in vivo.
source: Cell cycle synchronization is difficult to measure in cells in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field.

claim: AxFUCCI's property of labeling short, discrete landmarks in the cell cycle enabled visualization of high G1/S synchrony at 1 and 2 days post-amputation in vivo.
source: Here, AxFUCCI's property of labeling short, discrete landmarks in the cell cycle (e.g., G1/S transition) enabled us to visualize high G1/S synchrony at 1 and 2 days post-amputation in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary of how AxFUCCI enabled the observation of cell cycle synchrony.

claim: Significantly fewer ependymal cells were in S/G2 at baseline conditions in the present study compared to the previous study.
source: In particular, we found that significantly fewer ependymal cells were in S/G2 at baseline conditions in the present study compared to our previous study (Rost et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation comparing baseline conditions between studies.

claim: A dietary reduction could plausibly reduce baseline ependymal cell proliferation rate and animal growth.
source: The AxFUCCI experiments reported here were carried out under COVID-19-related operational restrictions – in particular, animal feeding frequency was reduced. A dietary reduction could plausibly reduce baseline ependymal cell proliferation rate and animal growth.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of observed differences.
